title: The benefit of uncertainty coupling in robust and adaptive robust optimization
contribution: Defines coupled uncertainty sets (a constraint-wise set intersected with a coupling set) and bounds the objective gain of coupling in static and adaptive robust optimization, linear and nonlinear, between shrinkage factors computable from the sets alone and shown tight on small instances; bounds the power of adaptability under coupling by a convex-program factor of at least 1/m; synthetic supply-chain, portfolio and lot-sizing runs track the bounds. Read: arXiv v2.
problem_entry: RO (LO and CP as engines): conservatism traced to constraint-wise sets that ignore couplings across constraints (abstract, p. 1; p. 2); coupled uncertainty only in toy and application-specific examples, 'a limited focus in the literature on the generic framework' (p. 2); the group's own adaptability bounds 'quite loose' or 'not necessarily tractable to compute' (p. 7); running supply-chain example, cost 600 -> 450 (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Shrinkage factors rho (largest inner scaling) and gamma (smallest outer scaling) between the constraint-wise set and the projections of the coupled set (static) or the coupled set itself (adaptive) sandwich the objective ratio (Definitions 3.3-3.5, Theorems 3.1-3.2, pp. 13-18); rho_adapt between the projection box and the coupled set bounds adaptive over static and is at least 1/m (Theorem 3.3, Lemma 3.5, pp. 21-22); the factors do not depend on the objective (p. 8).
assumptions: Linear RO/ARO with right-hand-side uncertainty in R^m_+ (pp. 9-12), coefficient uncertainty after translation to the point of symmetry so that {0} is in U (pp. 24-25), nonlinear problems under convexity or concavity with f(0) = 0 and g(0,0) = 0 (Assumptions 5.1-5.6, pp. 30-32); convex (compact) sets and positive finite optima (pp. 14, 18, 21); bounded recourse (Assumption 3.1, p. 21); fixed recourse for the nonlinear step (p. 48); down-hulls without loss of generality (p. 12; Lemma A.1, p. 45); synthetic data only: supply chain 50 instances, portfolio 100, lot sizing 50 (pp. 34-39); Gamma in 6.1 is a 2-norm radius (p. 34).
proof_devices: Scaling device: an optimal solution of one problem divided or multiplied by the shrinkage factor is feasible for the other and the objective scales with it (Theorems 3.1-3.2, pp. 15, 18-19; three-step summary, p. 29)
Down-hull reduction for right-hand-side uncertainty, so projections become boxes [0, d_i] (Definition 3.2, p. 12; p. 14; Lemma A.1, p. 45)
Closed-form factors from projection bounds (8), each bound a convex program (10) (pp. 14, 23); rho_aro and rho_adapt by convex robust programs (pp. 17, 22, 26-28); gamma_aro = gamma_ro (p. 18)
Tightness by two-dimensional instances with chosen costs, plus sufficient conditions for attainment (Corollaries 3.1.1-3.1.3, 3.2.1-3.2.2, 3.3.1, pp. 15-17, 19-20, 22; appendix, pp. 46-47, 53)
Adaptability bound via Ben-Tal et al. 2004 Theorem 2.1 on the projection box: zacp/zcp >= rho_adapt >= rho_aro/gamma_ro, and rho_adapt >= 1/m by convexity (Lemmas 3.4-3.5, Theorem 3.3, pp. 21-22)
q-norm coupling: rho_adapt = beta/(alpha m^(1/q)), tighter than the symmetry bound 1/(1 + m^(1/q)) and as tight as the non-convexity measure, computable by the convex program (9) (Example 3.4, p. 23)

Convexity or concavity with f(0) = 0 and g(0,0) = 0 gives one-sided nonlinear bounds; uncertainty in both objective and constraints squares the factors (Theorems 5.1-5.9, pp. 30-32; proofs, pp. 48-53)

Coupled robust counterpart through the support function of an intersection written as an infimal convolution, with m*l extra variables and constraints (Theorem D.1, p. 55); Fourier-Motzkin projections with cddlib (p. 54); cutting planes, decision-rule counterparts, Benders with outer approximation, hit-and-run scenarios (pp. 56-58)
experiments: Intel Xeon E5-2650, Python 3.6, Gurobi (version not stated), no time limits, Benders and cutting planes at 1,000 iterations and 1e-3 tolerance (pp. 33, 35, 38, 39); metrics zcp/zro, zacp/zaro and run time with one-standard-deviation bands (p. 33); supply chain M = 5 to 500 tracks the band [1 - alpha, 1] (Figure 9, p. 35), counterpart equals cutting planes on 100% of static instances (Figure 10, p. 36); portfolio to m = 140, 'neither one dominates' (Figure 11, p. 38); lot sizing: no static gain, adaptive gain about 1/sqrt(m), Benders a close lower bound under 100 s (Figure 12, p. 40); no violation or misspecification test, no real data, no code.
positioning: Coupling set against constraint-relaxing remedies (light robustness, globalized RO, robustness optimization) that 'do not address another main cause of conservatism' (pp. 5-6), against Roos-den Hertog aggregation (p. 6), Nohadani-Sharma multi-period sets (p. 7) and robust satisficing (p. 8); data-driven sets read as implicit coupling (p. 7); the group's own symmetry and non-convexity bounds beaten or matched (pp. 7, 23); Ben-Tal et al. 2004 as the hinge (pp. 2, 22).
writing: One toy supply-chain example recalled after every definition and theorem, including where coupling gives nothing (pp. 3-4, 10-11, 14-15, 18-19, 22); an 'Obtaining shrinkage factors' recipe after each theorem (pp. 14, 17, 22, 26-28); cross-section comparisons (pp. 29, 32); 'tight and easily computable' (pp. 8, 40); hedges 'might', 'possible relationships' (p. 2), 'sometimes significantly' (p. 41); no limitations or future-work paragraph (pp. 40-41); label slips (pp. 28-29, 35, 39, 46-47).
limits_future: Stated: projections intractable in high dimension (pp. 6, 54); one-sided nonlinear bounds (p. 32); no gain when projections do not shrink (pp. 10-11, 40). No future work (pp. 40-41). Unstated: the benefit is counted only in objective value and the protection lost under a misspecified coupling is never measured (p. 33); positive optima required; the symmetry-point translation maximizes the factors only 'for most cases' (p. 24).

method_links.note: The value of a modelling property is indexed by set-only, solution-independent factors computed by convex programs and shown tight; empirical ratios sit inside the theoretical band against alpha and Gamma; no-gain cases printed.

One-sided price: only the cost side of coupling is measured, not the protection a coupling assumption gives up (contrast card S001 in c07); the decision-maker gets an a priori screening of factors and cost coefficients, not a knob.
The coupled counterpart stays in the nominal class with m*l extra variables and constraints and 'similar computational complexity'; the boundary is printed for projections and full adaptivity.

RO form: the exact two-stage Benders method is warm-started from the static robust solution and bracketed by decision-rule upper bounds and Benders or sampling lower bounds, with vertex enumeration as ground truth at small sizes; no MIO certificate, and the bracket is shown only in plots.
Adaptive-RO programme continuity: the den Hertog book cited first, the group's own adaptability bounds as yardstick, its 2012 Benders algorithm (card S006 in c13) and 2016 lot-sizing settings reused.

coauthors: Liangyuan Na, Bartolomeo Stellato, Irina Wang (p. 1; no affiliations, acknowledgements or funding printed in this version)

quotes.text: Therefore, an a priori analysis of the problem coefficients and shrinkage factors of potential coupled sets may be informative for the decision-maker, before solving the optimization problem.
The coupled robust counterpart improves the objective while maintaining similar computational complexity as the constraint-wise robust counterpart.

title: Efficient domain adaptation of multimodal embeddings using constrastive learning
contribution: Trains a small per-modality nonlinear projection on frozen foundation-model embeddings with a label-supervised contrastive loss, raising F1 averaged over default-parameter classifiers on Hartford HealthCare EHR notes (diabetes, hypertension) and a movie dataset in under a minute on a CPU, while full fine-tuning stays 6 F1 points better at about 11 GPU hours; the best model per task barely changes (appendix). Read: arXiv v1.
problem_entry: ML+AP: hospitals' compute and privacy constraints: frozen embeddings too general and high-dimensional, fine-tuning needs GPUs and staff, sensitive data cannot go to cloud providers (pp. 1-2); binary classification from m modalities with frozen extractors (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: A one-hidden-layer ReLU projection (128 outputs) per modality or on the concatenation, trained by a pairwise sigmoid contrastive loss on label agreement with temperature 0.1, 'similar to the SimCLR loss'; foundation models run once and the stored embeddings are reused (pp. 2, 4; Table 1, p. 6).
assumptions: Binary labels only; frozen ClinicalBERT and GTE-Qwen2-7B (clinical) or BERT and ViT-16 (movies) extractors; proprietary EPIC EHRs of 4,000 HHC patients (History & Physical, progress note, ICD codes turned into text) under an IRB protocol, labels diabetes and hypertension (p. 5); mm-imdb, 3,606 movies, comedy vs drama (pp. 5-6); fixed hyperparameters (Table 1, p. 6); class imbalance not discussed (Tables 2, 8, pp. 6, 12).
proof_devices: n/a: no formulation, analysis or guarantee; the method content is loss (2) and the single vs per-modality design (p. 4); as extracted, both terms of (2) read log sigma of the same argument and the projection is f_j in the text but g_j in (2) (p. 4)
experiments: Unprojected, PCA-128 and contrastive arms, single or per-modality (p. 6); RF, XGBoost, CART, LR, RBF-SVC and MLP at default parameters (p. 6); 5-fold cross-validated F1, AUC and accuracy (pp. 6, 12-13); per-modality contrastive average F1 76.3 vs 58.3, 27.6 vs 19.8, 76.4 vs 56.2 (Table 2, p. 6); one timing run: F1 0.845 in 51 s on 8 CPU cores vs 0.818 unprojected vs 0.909 for full fine-tuning in 39,562 s on an A100 (Table 6, p. 8); the largest gains sit on degenerate default SVC baselines (F1 0.1, Table 12, p. 12) and best-model F1 is a near-tie (Table 9, p. 12); no code.
positioning: Label-supervised, frozen-backbone and modality-agnostic, set against unsupervised vision contrastive methods (SimCLR, SwAV, MoCo), pairing-based multimodal ones (CPC, CLIP, ConVIRT, ALIGN) and structure-bound clinical ones (Xia et al.) (p. 3); the group's own framework (Soenksen et al. 2022) is precedent and baseline, TabText justifies text serialisation (pp. 1, 3, 5-6); no supervised-contrastive, adapter, LoRA or linear-probe baselines cited (text search).
writing: 'novel' (pp. 1-2); headline gains 'of up to more than 20%' and 'by up to 20% or more' (p. 2), hedged by 'depending on the downstream model used' (pp. 2, 7); healthcare frame at both ends, 'an ideal setting' (p. 8); boilerplate impact statement (p. 8); many typos, 'Constrastive' in the title (p. 1); no limitations section (pp. 1-8).
limits_future: Stated: binary classification only (pp. 3, 8); full fine-tuning is 6 points better (p. 8). No future work (p. 8). Unstated: proprietary data, one timing run, default hyperparameters, best-model near-ties left to the appendix (p. 12), no interpretability or decision evaluation for a diagnostic use.

title: From Data to Uncertainty Sets: a Machine Learning Approach
contribution: Builds uncertainty sets from a trained predictor's loss around its covariate-based prediction, calibrates the radius by a validation-loss order statistic for a distribution-free violation bound (and a sharper sub-Gaussian bound for squared error with predicted variances), shows the sets coincide with KL, variation-distance, ellipsoidal and l1 sets, and on synthetic newsvendor, portfolio and shortest-path problems gets lower objective and regret than covariate-free and rival sets. Read: arXiv v1.
problem_entry: RO+DA+ML: prescriptive methods (SPO; his own Bertsimas-Kallus 2020) treat uncertain objectives in expectation and 'neither approach extends' to uncertain constraints, where satisfaction in expectation can mean frequent violation (abstract, pp. 1-2); covariate-driven RO rivals need Rademacher bounds and 240,000 validation points for a 90% guarantee (p. 2).
key_idea: The sublevel set of the trained model's loss around its prediction, U(X) = {y | l(y, f*(X)) <= rho} (eq. 3, p. 3); several models' losses combined by closed-form uncertainty weights sigma_j^2 = E[l_j] (Theorem 2.1, p. 5; eq. 5, p. 6); a mean-variance network gives a predicted ellipsoid (pp. 8-9); the radius is a validation-loss order statistic (Theorem 3.1, p. 10).
assumptions: g concave in y (pp. 2, 6); decisions are functions of X (p. 4); i.i.d. validation losses (p. 9); conditionally independent sub-Gaussian components with yhat in ri dom g (p. 11) and an LLN approximation in m for (13) (p. 12), justified by boundedness and separate models (p. 14); synthetic data as in Elmachtoub-Grigas, predictors with one hidden layer of 5 ReLU units (p. 15); newsvendor N = 2,000, test 10,000; portfolio 5 assets, N up to 10,000, test 100; shortest path on a 5x5 grid, N = 5,000, test 100 (pp. 15, 17, 20).
proof_devices: Closed-form uncertainty weights by termwise minimisation of alpha/sigma^2 + log sigma^2 at sigma^2 = alpha (Theorem 2.1, p. 5)

Binary-label identities: cross-entropy = KL divergence, hinge = 2 x variation distance, so the loss sets equal phi-divergence sets; misclassification loss gives the group's robust-classification set; squared error an ellipsoid, absolute error an l1 ball (Propositions 1-2, pp. 7-8)

Robust counterpart by conjugate duality, rho u l*(v/u, yhat) - g_*(v, x) <= 0, separable over summed losses, with a conjugate table (eqs. 6-7, Table 2, p. 8); cutting planes for the classification sets (p. 6)

Order-statistic rank argument: P(Z <= Z_(i)) = E[F(Z_(i))] with binomial-CDF monotonicity gives at least i/(N+1); radius Z_(ceil((N+1)(1-alpha))), tight for continuous losses (Theorem 3.1, pp. 9-11); the split-conformal argument, with conformal prediction uncited

Sub-Gaussian violation bound of Bertsimas-den Hertog-Pauphilet 2021 applied to the dual form (14)-(15), a minimisation over the unit circle (16) and a Jensen-gap correction (Theorem 3.2, pp. 11-14; three stated departures from exp(-rho^2/2), p. 12); last steps not re-derived
experiments: Objective at a guarantee level, regret and radii on independent test sets (p. 15); no solver, hardware or run times reported; newsvendor vs the KL phi-divergence set: objective 5.4-25.6 vs 27.9-28.0, regret 0.4-20.6 vs 22.1-22.6, relative information gain 95% -> 20% with noise (Tables 3-5, p. 16); portfolio vs classical ellipsoid, SPO, kNN and Predict-and-Calibrate: radii far smaller at low noise but larger at high noise (Table 6, p. 18; Figures 1-2, pp. 19-20); shortest path 'similar' in the body (p. 20) but MSE radii up to about 7x the classical ones (Table 7, p. 23); violation judged on 100 test samples; all three test problems carry objective uncertainty.
positioning: SPO and his own P2P credited and limited to objectives, P2P conceded to coincide with predict-then-optimize for linear objectives (pp. 1-2); Sun et al. and Tulabandhula-Rudin faulted for Rademacher guarantees needing vast validation data (p. 2); 'Remarkably' a generalisation of Ben-Tal-Nemirovski's ellipsoid (p. 2), coinciding with Ben-Tal et al. 2013 phi-divergence sets and the group's robust-classification set (p. 7); RO machinery from Ben-Tal-den Hertog-Vial 2015 and the group's 2021 guarantees (pp. 8-12); deep-learning uncertainty quantification (Kendall et al.; Nix-Weigend; Bishop; Skafte et al.) (pp. 4, 8); conformal prediction not cited.
writing: Abstract runs gap -> remedy -> set -> guarantees -> one headline number, radii 'up to one order of magnitude smaller' (p. 1); intuition before formalism (p. 3); 'Notice that' paragraphs link each construct to a classical set (pp. 6, 8, 9); hedges 'suggesting', 'may be because' (pp. 17-18); 'Proof. Proof' template artefacts (pp. 5, 7, 10, 12); five numbered contributions (pp. 2-3); one-paragraph conclusion (p. 21).
limits_future: Stated: guarantees need validation data (p. 4); gains shrink with noise and need data (pp. 17-19); Predict-and-Calibrate gets lower objectives without guarantees (p. 18). Future: stronger guarantees for more loss functions (p. 21). Unstated: synthetic data only, tiny predictors, a marginal rather than conditional-on-X guarantee (p. 9), no run times or code, the worst radius results in the appendix (pp. 20, 23).

method_links.note: The protection knob is set from data: the radius is a validation-loss order statistic for a target violation alpha (the correction the skill's Method 3 asks for); the price is shown as objective and regret against guarantee level per method; bad cases printed (Table 6 at high noise, Table 7).

Loss sets keep the nominal class (squared error -> ellipsoid 'as tractable as' the classical one; absolute error -> l1 ball; cross-entropy -> KL set), counterparts by conjugate duality, boundary printed (g concave in y).
Decisions (objective, regret) are scored on independent test data rather than prediction error; a covariate-information measure explains when learning helps.
No owner, current rule or real data; the baselines are rival methods on synthetic instances.
A new student carries the prescriptive-analytics and data-driven-RO lines into ML-based uncertainty sets, starting from a named limit of the P2P paper.

transferable: (D2) Build the uncertainty set as a sublevel set of the predictor's own training loss around its prediction; it needs no retraining and inherits the loss's convexity (pp. 3-4, 6-9).

(D4) Combine heterogeneous losses by dividing each by its expected loss on the training data (closed-form uncertainty weights; Theorem 2.1 and eq. 5, pp. 5-6).
(D4) Show that a new set coincides with known sets for standard losses (KL, variation distance, ellipsoid, l1 ball), so that existing counterparts and guarantees transfer (pp. 7-9).
(D5) Report objective and regret against the realised violation probability for every method on a common test set, with the guarantee level as the knob (Tables 4-5; Figures 1-2; pp. 16, 19-20).
(D5) Report a measure of how much the covariates inform the predictor (relative information gain) next to the decision results, to explain when the method helps (Table 3, pp. 16-17).
